 When Higher Minimum Wages Don’t Mean Higher Incomes
 New Research Finds Wage Increases Can Reduce Work Hours and Income for Some Women and Affect Infant Health
 October 27, 2026 
 By: 
 Julia Hinckley, JD 
 Print: 
 Print this page 
 Share: 
 Share this page on Twitter 
 Share this page on Facebook 
 Share this page on LinkedIn 
 Related Articles

 Cash Alone Isn’t Enough. Here’s What Research Says Families Need
 Campaigns to increase state and local minimum wages aim to improve the lives of low-wage workers and their families. But new research from LDI Fellow David Powell includes a surprising and concerning finding: For many women and their children, increases in the minimum wage can actually reduce household income and worsen birth outcomes.
 Powell and colleagues from Harvard, RAND, and SUNY studied the large minimum wage increases following the Great Recession (2010–2019) and found evidence that, on average, these changes economically harmed women ages 16 to 44. Minimum wage increases were associated with reductions in hours worked and full-time work and increases in WIC receipt among women giving birth, suggesting worsening financial circumstances for these workers.
 Past Evidence on Minimum Wage Effects on Employment and Health
 While the literature on older minimum wage increases found some evidence of negative employment effects, the evidence is mixed, and some economists strongly disagree. More recent research examining larger minimum wage changes has found not only industry-level job losses but also reductions in hours worked for certain subgroups, including workers with the lowest wages and education levels.
 Prior studies have also looked at the health effects of minimum wage changes, including effects on infants , and found that modest minimum wage hikes generally improve infant health and well-being. Analyses of infant health are critical to understanding the impact of social and economic policies because health in infancy can shape outcomes throughout life, including the economic mobility and health of future generations .
 Effect of Wage Changes in the Decade After the Great Recession
 From 2010 to 2019, 20 states increased their statutory minimum wages by more than 25%, including Maine and New York, which, along with the District of Columbia, raised their minimum wages by at least 60%.
 During the same period, several states made no changes. The authors examined how this variation affected employment and birth outcomes using administrative birth records and Census survey data on employment. The team used a statistical approach that compares changes across three dimensions to account for state-specific changes over time.
 Why Some Women and Their Newborns Are Affected Negatively
 Low-wage female workers are already overrepresented in part-time, low-hour, or flexible-schedule positions in service industries such as retail, hospitality, and health care support.
 In response to steep minimum wage increases, employers may adjust work hours by reducing available weekly shifts or trimming full-time positions down to part-time positions.
 For pregnant women or low-income households, losing just a few hours of work each week could negate the benefits of a higher hourly wage. In contrast to earlier research examining smaller minimum wage increases, which found positive health effects, the new study found small adverse effects on birth outcomes, including a reduction in the average birth weight, and a 3.4% increase in babies classified as small for gestational age (SGA).
 Size and Type of Wage Change Matters
 The authors note that the minimum wage changes they studied were not only larger than those examined in previous studies but also often established future wage targets to be reached gradually, with potential adjustments for inflation.
 This may lead employers to adjust their employment practices in anticipation of future wage increases. While the study measures the overall net effect of minimum wage policies, it cannot fully isolate the mechanisms that may operate in opposing directions, such as gains in hourly pay versus reductions in employment or work hours or changes in maternal stress or smoking behaviors. Previous research has found that minimum wage increases are associated with a higher prevalence of wage theft , especially among younger workers, and that employers sometimes add skill requirements , such as a high school diploma, disproportionately harming workers with the lowest levels of education.
 Key Limitations About the Findings
 The study does not distinguish between voluntary and involuntary reductions in work hours, nor does it directly measure household earnings or resources. Instead, it uses reductions in full-time employment and work hours, along with increased participation in the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC), as indicators of worsening economic circumstances. 
 Considerations for Policymakers Who Want to Improve Economic Outcomes
 Given their findings, the authors suggest that policymakers considering large minimum wage increases should also consider pairing the change with interventions that could buffer the adverse employment and health effects documented in the study.
 These measures could include more targeted income support for pregnant women or expanded prenatal services. The authors also note that alternative policies, such as earned income tax credits, may improve economic well-being for low-wage families without the adverse health and employment effects associated with large minimum wage increases.
 The study, “ Recent Minimum Wage Policy and Its Impact on Birth Outcomes ,” was published in the the Journal of Health Economics on September 13, 2026. Authors include Yuji Mizushima, David Powell , Margaret Weden, Kate Strully, and Allison Appleton.
